{{Short description|American mathematician (1937–2017)}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=July 2025}}
[[Image:Charles Sims.jpg|thumb|180px|Charles C. Sims at [[Mathematical Research Institute of Oberwolfach|Oberwolfach]] in 2006]]

'''Charles Coffin Sims''' (April 14, 1937 – October 23, 2017<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/name/charles-sims-obituary?pid=187073829|title=Charles Coffin Sims|publisher=Legacy|accessdate=26 July 2019}}</ref><ref name=MacT>J. J. O'Connor and [[Edmund F. Robertson|E. F. Robertson]], [http://www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Sims.html ''Charles Sims biography''], [[MacTutor History of Mathematics archive]]. Accessed 2018-12-20.</ref>) was an American [[mathematician]] best known for his work in [[group theory]].<ref name="obit">{{Cite web |url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/app/obituary.aspx?n=charles-coffin-sims&pid=187073829&fhid=5590 |title=Charles Coffin Sims's Obituary  |website=Asbury Park Press |access-date=2017-11-04}}</ref> Together with [[Donald G. Higman]] he discovered the [[Higman–Sims group]], one of the [[sporadic group]]s.  The [[permutation group]] software developed by Sims also led to the proof of existence of the [[Lyons group]] (also known as the Lyons–Sims group) and the [[O'Nan group]] (also known as the O'Nan–Sims group).

Sims was born and raised in [[Elkhart, Indiana]], and received his [[B.S.]] from the [[University of Michigan]].<ref name="obit"/> He did his graduate studies at [[Harvard University]], where he was a student of [[John G. Thompson]] and received his [[Ph.D.]] degree in 1963.  In his thesis, he enumerated [[p-group|''p''-group]]s, giving sharp asymptotic upper and lower bounds.  Sims is one of the founders of [[computational group theory]] and is the [[eponym]] of the [[Schreier–Sims algorithm]]. He was a faculty member at the Department of Mathematics at [[Rutgers University–New Brunswick|Rutgers University]] from 1965 to 2007. During that period he served, in particular, as Department Chair (1982–84) and Associate Provost for Computer Planning (1984–87). Sims retired from Rutgers in 2007 and moved to [[St. Petersburg, Florida|St. Petersburg]], Florida.<ref>[http://math.rutgers.edu/newsletter/newsletter2007.html#retirements ''Spring 2007 Newsletter.''] Department of Mathematics, [[Rutgers University]]. Accessed November 1, 2008.</ref>

In 2012, he became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[http://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 2013-07-20.</ref>
